items.title: Give every quantity a job
items.chapter: Read the question into a useful model
items.transcript: When a maths problem gives you three numbers, each number can do a different job. One might count packets. Another might tell you how many counters fit in each packet. The third might count counters on their own. Give every number its job before you calculate. Start with the question: how many counters altogether? That tells us the unit of our answer. Four plus three plus two gives nine, but we would be adding a packet count to two different descriptions of counters. Give each quantity its label and ask what it would take to get everything into counters. Mia has four packets of counters. Each packet contains three counters, and Mia has two loose counters as well. How many counters does she have altogether? Before you work it out, point to what the four, the three and the two each describe. Four tells us how many groups there are. Three tells us the size of every group. Open the first packet and you can see three counters. Open the others and the same group repeats. Four groups of three give twelve counters. Multiplication gives the counter total for the packets. The two loose counters are already in the unit we want. Slide them into the collection. Now we are adding twelve counters and two counters, and the total is fourteen counters. Check it in the picture: four rows of three, and two beside them. The same idea works with measurements. One ribbon is two metres long, and another is thirty centimetres long. How much ribbon is there altogether? Two metres is two hundred centimetres. Both lengths are now in centimetres, so together they measure two hundred and thirty centimetres. A number can have a different job even when it uses the same digits. Think of a book with pages numbered ninety-five through one hundred and five. In just that range, how many times is the digit nine written? Look across the page numbers and find each printed nine. Five page numbers contain a nine: ninety-five, ninety-six, ninety-seven, ninety-eight and ninety-nine. The last page number on that list contains two nines. Its first nine counts once and its second nine counts once. There are six written nines in all. Read the final question. Label each number with what it counts or measures. Bring quantities into a common unit when you need to add them. Here is your notebook challenge. Six boxes hold eight pencils each. Five pencils are broken. How many unbroken pencils are there? Label the quantities and show your calculation.

items.title: Choose a representation that exposes the relationship
items.chapter: Read the question into a useful model
items.transcript: A difficult-looking question can become much clearer as soon as you draw the right picture. A line shows order. A table sets comparisons side by side. A sketch makes shapes and boundaries visible. An equation holds a relationship in place. Choose the one that helps you see what the question is asking. Picture a fence. Your eye can follow every post or every panel between two posts. A sketch gives both counts a place on the same line. The words each end tell us where the fence starts and stops. Mark those ends first. Then look for what repeats between them. A straight fence is thirty metres long. There is a post at each end, and the posts are five metres apart. How many posts are there? Draw the full thirty metres. Mark the left end as zero, and mark off spaces of five metres. Thirty metres divided into five-metre spaces gives six gaps. Follow each gap to its right-hand end. That accounts for six posts. The post at zero sits before the first gap, so add it once. Six gaps, plus that starting post, makes seven posts. Now join the ends to make a closed fence, using the same six equal panels. Watch the last post come back to the very first one. They meet at a single corner. Each panel now ends at a different post, and all posts are included. That makes six gaps and six posts. Try the same kind of line with a queue. Sam is ninth from the front and sixth from the back. How many people are there? Eight stand in front of Sam, and five stand behind. Eight, plus Sam, plus five, makes fourteen. Both ranks include Sam, so give Sam one place in the picture. A table helps when there are several things to compare. Box A contains eight pencils and costs sixteen dollars. Box B contains four pencils and costs twelve dollars. Add a price per pencil column. The divisions give two dollars and three dollars. Box A costs more for the box and less for each pencil. A sketch reveals a boundary. Join two mats, each four metres by three metres, along their three-metre sides. How much edge is exposed? Each mat has fourteen metres around it. The pair has twenty-eight before joining. The shared edge removes three metres from each mat, so the equation gives twenty-two metres outside. Choose a line for order and gaps, a table for comparisons, and a sketch for shape and boundaries. Use an equation to show how the quantities fit together. Your turn. Trees are planted every four metres along a forty-metre path, including both ends. How many trees are there? Sketch it first.

items.title: Use the model to check the answer
items.chapter: Read the question into a useful model
items.transcript: Imagine a calculation gives seven and a half people in a queue. A headcount has to be a whole number. That tells you to look back at your reasoning. Start problems by asking what a sensible answer could look like. Then use that idea to check the result. A count of buses is a whole number. A probability is between zero and one, including both ends. An area has square units. Three metres along each side of a square gives nine square metres. Identify the kind of answer first. The model also helps you predict its size. One hundred and thirty students are going on a trip. Each bus has seats for forty students. What is the smallest number of buses that can take the whole group? Make a quick estimate before you continue. Think about what happens if a bus is only partly full. Group the students into forties. One bus takes forty. A second takes another forty. A third brings the total on board to one hundred and twenty. There are still ten students waiting. Write one hundred and thirty as three lots of forty plus ten. Those ten students still need seats. Put them in a fourth bus. Ten of its forty seats are used, so thirty are spare. Everyone now has a seat, and the answer is four buses. Check both sides of the boundary. Four buses make one hundred and sixty seats, enough for all one hundred and thirty students. Three buses make one hundred and twenty seats, so ten students would be left out. Any smaller number has even fewer seats. Four is the smallest number that works. Keep the same trip. This time ask how many buses are completely full if the driver fills each bus before opening the next. Each of the first three has forty students. The fourth has ten. So three buses are full. The last sentence of the question tells you which count to give. Predict what a sensible answer should look like. Check every condition, then reread the question. Here is your notebook challenge. Pack one hundred eggs into boxes of twelve. Fill each box before opening the next. How many boxes are needed, and how many eggs go in the last box?

items.title: Read the question into a useful model
items.chapter: Read the question into a useful model
items.transcript: A ribbon lies along a centimetre ruler. Its left edge lines up with two, and its right edge lines up with nine. How long is the ribbon? Look at where it begins and ends, then try to explain your first move. The mark labelled two is two centimetres from zero. The mark labelled nine is nine centimetres from zero. The question asks for the distance from the first position to the second. Trace that part of the ruler with your finger. Move from two to three. That is the first centimetre. From three to four is the second. Every small step adds one centimetre. Keep going until you reach nine. There are seven gaps of one centimetre, so the ribbon is seven centimetres long. The nine centimetres from zero to the end includes two centimetres before the ribbon begins. Remove those two centimetres. Nine minus two leaves seven. You can count eight marked points across the ribbon because both ends have a mark. Each centimetre lives in the space between two marks. Slide the ribbon two centimetres to the left. Watch both ends move the same distance. It starts at zero and reaches seven. The two endpoints changed together, and the span stayed seven centimetres. That is another way to check our answer. The same idea works with time. A film starts at seven fifteen in the evening and ends at nine oh five. How many minutes pass? Draw a timeline. Put seven fifteen on the left. Mark eight o'clock and nine o'clock along the way, and stop at nine oh five. From seven fifteen to eight o'clock is forty-five minutes. The next hour gives sixty minutes. From nine o'clock to the end is five more. Add forty-five, sixty and five. The total is one hundred and ten minutes. That is one hour and fifty minutes. Label the two positions. Find the length, or the time, between them. Use equal steps and check the units. Now try your own timeline. A camera starts filming at ten forty-seven in the morning and stops at twelve oh six that day. How many minutes does it record?

items.title: Find an invariant by inspecting one move
items.chapter: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: Here's a puzzle. One pile has five gold counters. The other has seven blue counters. You may move counters between the piles, as often as you like. Could you finish with ten counters in each pile? Before you try dozens of moves, ask a better question. Is there something that no legal move can change? Watch closely. Move two blue counters to the gold pile. Now there are seven on the left and five on the right. The picture has changed, but the total is still twelve. Every transfer takes some counters away from one pile and adds exactly that many to the other. Nothing is created. Nothing disappears. So ten and ten is impossible. That would require twenty counters, and we have only twelve. Six and six, however, is possible. A quantity that remains unchanged after every permitted move is called an invariant. Here, the invariant is the total number of counters. But here's the twist. Change the rule. Each move now adds two brand-new counters to both piles. What stays fixed this time? The total is growing, by four with every move. So the total is no longer an invariant. Look at the difference between the two piles instead. We begin with five and seven: a gap of two. Add two to each and we get seven and nine. Add two again, and we get nine and eleven. The gap is always two. Let's prove this, rather than just spot a pattern. Call the two pile sizes A and B. After a move, their sizes are A plus two and B plus two. Now subtract the new sizes. The positive two and negative two cancel perfectly. We are left with A minus B. So the difference cannot change. Go back to transferring counters. If the first pile loses t and the second gains t, the total becomes A minus t, plus B plus t. Again, the changes cancel. Here's the important trap. Moving counters preserves the total, but not usually the difference. Adding the same number to both preserves their difference, but changes the total. Try one yourself. Start with four counters in one pile and nine in the other. Each move adds two counters to both. Could you reach eighteen and twenty-three? Yes. The difference starts at five and ends at five. Exactly seven moves add fourteen counters to each pile. Both target numbers work. But could you reach eighteen and twenty-two? No. Their difference is four, not five. The invariant rules that out instantly. This is the power of an invariant. You don't need to simulate a hundred moves. Examine one move, identify what cancels, and use that to reason about every move. Pause here. Draw one move in your notebook, and write a single equation showing what remains unchanged.
items.extended_reading: This section is called Find an invariant by inspecting one move. An invariant is a quantity that does not change when a permitted move is made. It might be a total, a difference, a product, a remainder or a colour balance. Start by comparing the state immediately before and immediately after one move. A claim about a long process becomes much easier to justify if every individual move preserves the same quantity. SEE IT Two moves, two different invariants A transfer moves existing units between piles, so their total stays fixed. Adding two new units to each pile preserves the difference instead. A transfer between two piles preserves their combined total. If t is transferred from the first pile to the second, the signed difference “first minus second” decreases by 2t. To find the absolute gap, also check whether the piles exchange order. By contrast, adding the same amount to both piles preserves their difference but changes their total. Naming the operation prevents these two situations from being confused. A038 and A112 are useful places to look for a preserved difference rather than solve several unrelated unknowns. If objects come in two types with different per-object contributions, compare the real collection with a starting model made entirely from one type. Keep the object count fixed. Each replacement changes the total by the same difference, so the total change determines how many replacements occurred. Check both the object count and the final total. A014 and A056 fit this comparison method. Sometimes the visible entries are not the quantities worth tracking. Try a small adjustment such as adding or subtracting a fixed amount from each entry. Expand the rule and look for cancellation or factorisation. N1.26 invites this kind of search. The important proof has two parts: identify a candidate quantity, then show algebraically that one legal move leaves it unchanged. A pattern noticed in a few trials is only a clue. Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. Then draw the smallest model, table or example that would help you recognise the same idea in a new problem.

items.title: Work backwards: undo the last move first
items.chapter: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: Sometimes a maths puzzle tells you the finish, but hides the start. Working backwards means beginning with that finish and undoing the moves. There is one crucial rule: undo the last move first. Like taking off your shoes before your socks, the order matters. This is useful when guessing the starting number would take ages. If each move can be undone, we can follow a clear route back to the start. Then we check the answer by travelling forwards again. Let's try a number machine. It multiplies a secret number by four, then adds three. The machine finishes at twenty-three. What number went in? Notice the order: multiply first, then add. Start at twenty-three. The last thing the machine did was add three, so undo that first. Twenty-three minus three is twenty. We have recovered the amount just before the final addition. Only now do we undo the multiplication. Twenty divided by four is five. Check the whole journey: five times four is twenty, and twenty plus three is twenty-three. Five works. What if we undo the operations in the wrong order? Twenty-three divided by four is five point seven five. Subtract three, and we get two point seven five. That is not five. The order is part of the method. Here is why the correct order works for any starting number. Call the start x. The machine makes four x plus three. Subtracting three leaves four x. Dividing by four leaves x. We peel away the outside operation first. Multiplying by zero would lose the starting information, so that move cannot be undone uniquely. Now try a different kind of puzzle. A child keeps half of a collection of counters. Then they keep two thirds of what remains. At the end, there are eight counters. How many were there at the start? Work backwards from eight. These eight counters are two thirds of the previous pile. Split them into two equal groups of four. Restore the missing third, another group of four. The previous pile had twelve counters. Twelve was half of the original collection. Double it to recover twenty-four. Now check forwards. Half of twenty-four is twelve. Two thirds of twelve is eight. Every stage agrees. The common trap is using the wrong whole. Two thirds of what remains means two thirds of twelve, not two thirds of the original twenty-four. Write the amount after every stage so the whole stays clear. There is one more check when a puzzle uses whole counters. Every intermediate pile must also be whole. Suppose a rule halves the pile, adds one counter, then doubles it. Could the final pile contain seven? Undo the steps. Seven divided by two is three point five. Subtract one to get two point five. Double it to get five. The starting number is whole, but the intermediate piles are not. You cannot have half a counter in this puzzle. So seven is impossible under these rules. Try eight instead. Backwards, eight becomes four, then three, then six. Forwards, six becomes three, then four, then eight. Every pile is whole, and every move is legal. Remember the method. Reverse the order. Undo each operation. Check every intermediate state. Then check the complete forward journey. A backward calculation finds a candidate; the checks show whether it really works. Your turn. A number is multiplied by three, then four is subtracted. The result is seventeen. Pause here. Recover the starting number, then draw the forward journey to prove your answer.

items.title: Compare different orders of the same operations
items.chapter: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: Start with three. Add two and then double. Five becomes ten. Try the same start with the operations swapped. Double three first, then add two. Six becomes eight. The same steps can give different results when their order changes. Testing more starting numbers might help us guess a pattern. A letter lets us explain the pattern for every starting number. We'll compare the two operation orders side by side and look for the part that changes. Choose any starting number. Order A adds five and then doubles. Order B doubles and then adds five. Which order gives the bigger result, and by how much? Try one starting number before we compare them all. Call the starting number x. In Order A, adding five makes a bar with an x part and a five part. Doubling makes two copies of that whole bar. Collect its parts. Two copies of x and two fives give two x plus ten. Order B doubles x first. That gives two copies of x. Add five once. Both orders now show two copies of the starting value and at least one five. Pair those matching pieces. The extra five in Order A is the entire difference. What if we multiply by negative two instead? In Order A, the five is multiplied too, so its contribution is negative ten. Order B still adds positive five. The common part is negative two x in both orders. Positive five is fifteen more than negative ten, so Order B now wins by fifteen. Two additions can swap because we still add the same total. Two multiplications can swap because their combined scale is the same. When you mix the two types of step, look closely at whether an amount added later gets scaled at all. Give the start a letter. Write the two orders separately. Compare the parts that match and calculate the difference. In your notebook, compare subtracting four and then multiplying by three with multiplying by three and then subtracting four. Which gives the greater result, and by how much?

items.title: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.chapter: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: Start with any whole number, including zero. Rule A adds three and then multiplies by four. Rule B multiplies by four and then adds three. Which output is larger, and by how much? Sketch one example before looking for a proof. Call the start x. Rule A forms x plus three and makes four copies of the whole amount. Look at one copy. It contains an x tile and a three tile. Four copies give four x tiles and four threes, so the result is four x plus twelve. In Rule B, the multiplication acts on the starting value. Make four copies of x. Now add the three. This time the three comes in once, after the copying step. The result is four x plus three. Line up the outputs. Each side contains four copies of the same x and one added three. Pair those tiles. There are three extra threes in Rule A. Their total is nine. Whatever whole number we pick at the start, Rule A is larger by nine. Check the smallest allowed input. Starting from zero gives twelve and three. Starting from ten gives fifty-two and forty-three. Each difference is nine. In both rows, the starting amount changes the two outputs by the same amount. The multiplication makes extra copies of the added amount when the addition comes first. Use that observation with two new rules. One adds two before multiplying by six. The other multiplies by six before adding two. Draw the matching pieces and find the gap.

items.title: Read a remainder as a precise statement
items.chapter: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: Seventeen counters make three full groups of five, with two left over. That leftover is called the remainder. The three full groups give a multiple of five. The two counters tell you exactly how far seventeen is past that multiple. When we divide whole numbers by five, the possible remainders are zero, one, two, three and four. A leftover of five would make another complete group. However large the starting number, it fits into one of these five remainder classes. A necklace repeats red, blue, green and yellow in that order. The first bead is red. What colour is bead fifty? Try marking the boundaries between the repeating groups of four. A full cycle has four beads. Fifty is twelve groups of four, plus two more beads. The twelve groups take us to bead forty-eight. Count two beads into the next cycle. Its second colour is blue, so bead fifty is blue. Bead forty-eight lands on a complete group boundary. It has remainder zero when divided by four. In this position list we count from one, so a complete group finishes on its fourth bead. Bead forty-eight is yellow. Twenty-three is four groups of five plus three. Thirty-eight is seven groups of five plus three. In the difference, the two leftovers cancel. Three extra groups of five give fifteen. And adding any whole group of five leaves a remainder unchanged. That is why equal remainders and a multiple-of-five difference go together. Try combining two conditions. Below thirty, the numbers with remainder three on division by five are three, eight, thirteen, eighteen, twenty-three and twenty-eight. Now test them for remainder one on division by three. Only thirteen and twenty-eight reach that column. A remainder tells how far you are past a multiple. It must be smaller than the divisor. For a repeating pattern, decide which position sits at remainder zero. Here is your notebook challenge. Today is Tuesday. What day will it be one hundred days from now?

items.title: Separate the first coincidence from the repeat period
items.chapter: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: Two lights repeat at different speeds. One flashes every four seconds and the other every six. We can ask when they first flash together after starting. We can also ask how much time separates one meeting from the next. Twenty-four is a multiple of both four and six. A smaller common multiple may also work. First mark where each light starts. Then add its own period each time. A timeline shows both the starting positions and the repeated jumps. Both lights flash at time zero. One repeats every four seconds. The other repeats every six seconds. When do they next flash together? List a few times for each light, and line up the lists. The first light flashes at four, eight, twelve and sixteen. The second flashes at six, twelve and eighteen. Their first positive meeting is at twelve seconds. Twelve is the lowest common multiple of four and six. A gap between meetings has to be a multiple of both periods, so the next meeting is twelve seconds later. Let the second light start at time two. Its times are two, eight, fourteen and twenty. The first light's times stay on the multiples of four. The first meeting moves to eight seconds, and the next is at twenty. The starting offset changed the first meeting. The twelve-second gap stayed the same. Now start the second light at time one. Its jumps of six keep all its times odd. Starting from zero and moving in jumps of four keeps the other times even. An odd time and an even time cannot match, so these two lights never flash together. When meetings are possible, the lowest common multiple gives the gap between them. The starting positions decide when the first meeting happens. In your notebook, one bus leaves every eight minutes and another every twelve. They both leave at nine o'clock. When do they next leave together?

items.title: Build guarantees with the pigeonhole principle
items.chapter: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: Put four counters into three boxes. You can place the first three with one in each box. The fourth has to join a counter somewhere. If you already put two together earlier, the claim already holds. This is the pigeonhole principle. A guarantee asks what must happen in every possible case. Imagine the arrangement that delays the result for as long as possible. Its limit helps us find the smallest count that will force the result. The important decision is what the boxes represent. A drawer contains many socks of exactly four colours. You take socks without looking. What is the smallest number you must take to guarantee two of the same colour? Try to plan a draw that delays the first matching pair. Use one box for each colour. Begin with one sock in each box. That is a possible draw of four socks with no match. The fifth sock has to go into one of the occupied boxes. Five is sufficient, and this example with four proves that five is the minimum. The boxes can stand for remainders. Take any four different whole numbers. When we divide by three, the possibilities are zero, one and two. Two of the four numbers share a remainder. Take their difference. The leftover parts cancel, leaving a multiple of three. Choose six different numbers from one to ten. Group the ten numbers into five pairs that add to eleven. A choice of six puts two numbers in one of those five pair boxes. Both members of that pair have been chosen, and they add to eleven. Choose the objects and choose the boxes. Compare their counts. When the problem asks for the smallest guarantee, show how one fewer could fail. In your notebook, how many people must be in a room to guarantee two birthdays in the same month?

items.title: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.chapter: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: Choose any four different whole numbers. Prove that two of them always have a difference that is a multiple of three. You can choose very large numbers if you like. How can one argument cover every possible choice? Divide a whole number by three. The remainder can be zero, one or two. A leftover of three would make another complete group. Create one box for each of the three allowable remainders. Every chosen number belongs to exactly one box. Four numbers and three boxes force at least two numbers into the same box. Those two numbers have the same remainder. We can use that single fact to show their difference is a multiple of three. Write the larger number as three a plus r, and the smaller as three b plus the same r. On subtracting, the two r terms cancel. The result is three times the difference between a and b. It is a whole number of groups of three. Try two, six, ten and thirteen. Ten and thirteen both leave remainder one. Their difference is three. Could three numbers guarantee the result? With one, two and three, the remainders all differ. Their differences are one or two. This shows four is the smallest number that guarantees a match. Choose a box for each remainder and use subtraction once two numbers share a box. Now increase the divisor to ten. How many different whole numbers guarantee that two differ by a multiple of ten? Show both why your answer works and how one fewer choice could fail.

items.title: Factor with a purpose
items.chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.transcript: Whole numbers bigger than one are made by multiplying primes. A prime has exactly two positive factors, one and itself. Take sixty. Split it into six and ten, then split those again. The prime pieces are two, three, two and five. Start another way. Write sixty as four times fifteen. Four gives two twos, and fifteen gives a three and a five. Rearrange the pieces in increasing order and both trees give the same list. That fixed prime factorisation is why we can work with the pieces. Is ninety-one prime? Decide which small primes you would try first, and think about how far the search needs to go. Ninety-one is odd, so two fails. Its digits add to ten, so three fails. Its last digit is one, so five fails. Try seven. Seven times thirteen equals ninety-one. These two factors show that ninety-one is composite. If both factors were bigger than the square root, multiplying them would give too much. So a composite number has a prime factor at or below its square root. For ninety-seven that root lies between nine and ten. Try two, three, five and seven. All leave a remainder, so ninety-seven is prime. Three different whole numbers, each bigger than one, multiply to sixty-six. Which numbers are they? Sixty-six has exactly three prime pieces, two, three and eleven. Each of the three numbers needs a piece. Each gets exactly one, so those three primes are the answer. Split a number until all its pieces are prime. When you test whether a number is prime, use the small primes up to its square root. One has only one positive factor. In your notebook, write eighty-four as a product of primes.

items.title: Count divisors by making independent choices
items.chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.transcript: Twelve has six positive factors: one, two, three, four, six and twelve. We can list those by finding the products that make twelve. For a larger number, it is easier to count choices from its prime factorisation. Three hundred and sixty factorises into two cubed, three squared and five. Its full factor list has twenty-four entries. We can account for them through three small counts, one for each prime. Let's see how this works with twelve first. Twelve is two times two times three. A factor of twelve is made from some of those prime tiles. Think about how many twos you can use. Then think about your choices for the three. How many different products are possible? Use zero, one or two twos. That gives three choices. For each of them, either include the three or leave it out. That gives two choices. Three times two makes six products. Taking no tiles gives one. Taking all the tiles gives twelve. Every cell makes a different factor. Seventy-two is two cubed times three squared. Choose zero, one, two or three twos. For each choice there are three possibilities for the threes. Four times three gives twelve factors. For three hundred and sixty, the extra choice about the five doubles that count to twenty-four. For thirty-six, the factor pairs are one and thirty-six, two and eighteen, three and twelve, and four and nine. Six pairs with itself, so it appears just once in the list. A factor pairs with itself exactly when its square is the number. That is why square numbers have an odd count of positive factors. For each prime, include the choice to use zero copies. Add one to the prime's exponent, and multiply the resulting counts. In your notebook, find the number of positive factors of two hundred, then explain why your method counts each factor once.

items.title: Track prime copies through several conditions
items.chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.transcript: Write twelve as two times two times three. Write eighteen as two times three times three. Group copies of the same prime vertically. One column holds the twos. Another holds the threes. We can see exactly how many of each prime each number uses. We can solve three problems using these counts. To divide into both numbers, a factor needs to fit inside both rows. A common multiple has to contain both rows. For a square, the tiles must split into two matching sets. Find the largest positive number that divides both twelve and eighteen. Then find the smallest positive number that is a multiple of both. Use the tiles, and decide how many copies of each prime you need. A common factor can use only the copies both numbers can supply. Eighteen can supply one two and twelve can supply one three. Those are the smaller counts in the two columns. The highest common factor is two times three, which is six. A common multiple needs enough copies to cover either number. Twelve needs two twos. Eighteen needs two threes. Take the larger count in each column. Two twos and two threes multiply to thirty-six. It is the lowest common multiple. For each prime, the smaller count plus the larger count equals the original two counts added together. So the factors of six and thirty-six together use exactly the same prime copies as twelve and eighteen together. Both products are two hundred and sixteen. A square needs two matching groups of prime tiles. Thirty-six splits into two sixes. Forty-eight has four twos and one three. The three has no partner. Multiply by another three and the tiles can split evenly. The new total is one hundred and forty-four, or twelve squared. Use the smaller prime counts for a highest common factor. Use the larger counts for a lowest common multiple. A square has even counts of every prime. In your notebook, find the highest common factor and lowest common multiple of twenty and thirty.

items.title: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.chapter: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.transcript: What is the smallest positive whole number that you can multiply ninety by to make a perfect square? Try to think of ninety as a collection of prime pieces. A square will let those pieces split into two identical groups. Ninety factorises into two times three times three times five. Each prime needs an even number of copies in a square. The threes already make a pair. The two and the five each appear once. Put a space for a partner beside each of them. Supply one more two and one more five. Those are the missing tiles. Their product is ten, so multiplying ninety by ten adds just the two partners we need. Now each prime has an even count. Ninety times ten is nine hundred. Split its tiles into two identical groups, each with a two, a three and a five. Each group multiplies to thirty. Thirty times thirty is nine hundred, so the new number is a square. Could a smaller positive multiplier work? Any multiplier that works must supply a two and a five, because those counts start odd. A number divisible by the two distinct primes two and five is a multiple of ten. Ten is the first positive multiple and we have shown it works. For a square, pair every prime. Choose one partner for each prime whose count is odd. Try the same proof with sixty. Find the smallest positive whole number to multiply sixty by to make a square, and check your answer by splitting the new prime tiles into two equal groups.

items.title: Decide whether order belongs to the outcome
items.chapter: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.transcript: This section is called Decide whether order belongs to the outcome. If positions or roles are different, exchanging two objects usually creates a new outcome. If only membership matters, exchanging the order in which members were chosen does not. Write that distinction explicitly. Selecting people for named jobs is different from selecting an unranked team. In A126, the wording determines which choices have order and which do not. SEE IT Explain why division by two works For the three different objects A, B and C, each two-object group has two orders. The six ordered choices merge in equal-sized groups of two. For n different objects in a row, there are n choices for the first place, n-1 for the second, and so on. Their product is written n!, pronounced “n factorial”. To select an unordered pair, the ordered count n(n-1) counts every pair twice, once in each order, so divide by two. The justification for division is equal repeated counting, not a vague sense that the first total is too large. More generally, C(n, k) denotes the number of ways to choose k different objects from n different objects when order does not matter. For integers 0 ≤ k ≤ n, first count ordered selections: n(n-1)⋯(n-k+1). Each selected group appears in k! orders, so C(n, k) = n!/[k!(n-k)!]. There is one empty selection, so C(n, 0) = 1 and 0! = 1. If k > n, there is no such selection and C(n, k) = 0. Repeated objects need the same care. Temporarily labelling identical objects makes them different, which may overcount the printed arrangements. Before dividing, establish how many labelled versions every unlabelled arrangement has. If that number varies from outcome to outcome, one division cannot repair the count. A099 and N4.28 give useful practice in deciding whether the object being counted is an arrangement, an operation history or a final result. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Split by the restriction that changes the choices
items.chapter: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.transcript: This section is called Split by the restriction that changes the choices. A useful case division has two properties: the cases cannot overlap, and together they cover every legal outcome. Choose a feature that controls the remaining choices. In a digit problem, the last digit or the position of zero may be more restrictive than the first digit. Fixing that feature can turn a confusing count into several straightforward products. SEE IT A complement needs a visible universe Each switch has two states, so the universe has four complete outcomes. Only ON, ON is forbidden; subtracting it leaves three. Multiply within a case when successive choices build one complete outcome. Add across disjoint cases. Do not assume every case has the same number of choices. A leading-zero rule, a required neighbour or a fixed position can make one branch smaller than another. A095 and A101 are useful for reading such restrictions without replacing them by a more familiar but different question. Sometimes it is easier to count everything and subtract the forbidden outcomes. This complement method needs a clear universe: what exactly is included in “everything”? If two forbidden conditions can occur together, subtracting their counts separately may remove an outcome twice. Either separate them into disjoint classes or restore the overlap. A048 is a place to compare direct counting with a carefully defined complement. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Prove that the classification is reversible
items.chapter: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.transcript: This section is called Prove that the classification is reversible. A strong counting method gives each outcome an address in your list of cases. From an outcome, you should be able to recover the choices that produced it. Conversely, every allowed choice in the method should build a valid outcome. This two-way check proves completeness and prevents double counting. It is often more convincing than a second long multiplication. Neighbour restrictions can sometimes be handled by placing separator objects first and using the gaps around them. Restrictions on misplaced objects can be handled by describing how positions send objects around cycles. N2.26 and N1.27 develop these different representations. The representation must capture the actual rule; the same convenient picture should not be reused when a changed condition invalidates it. Be especially careful when several action histories can produce one final object. Classify the final structures, or identify precisely which histories merge together. N4.28 asks for this distinction. For an independent check, list the smallest meaningful cases or use a different classification. A computer enumeration can confirm a count, but the written explanation should still make clear why every legal outcome has one place in the argument. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.chapter: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Count outcomes once, using complete cases. Let the restriction split the cases A lunch contains one sandwich, cheese or bean, and one fruit, apple, pear or plum. Cheese may not be paired with plum. How many different legal lunches are there? The branches have different sizes because the restriction affects only cheese. Multiply the numbers of choices within each case, then add the disjoint case totals. Work through the example 1. Split by sandwich. These cases cannot overlap because a lunch contains exactly one sandwich. 2. With cheese, the permitted fruits are apple and pear: two lunches. 3. With bean, all three fruits are permitted: three lunches. 4. Add the disjoint cases: 2+3=5. Each leaf names its sandwich and fruit, so every legal lunch appears exactly once. As a check, 2 times 3-1=5 counts all pairs and removes cheese with plum. Answer. There are 5 different legal lunches. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. items.title: Count incidences before counting objects
items.chapter: Count the same structure from two directions
items.transcript: This section is called Count incidences before counting objects. An incidence is a meeting between an object and one of its features: a bridge and an endpoint, a shape and an edge, or a member and a group. You do not need to remember the word to use the idea. Ask what is being counted when each local object reports its own contribution, and how many reports refer to the same underlying thing. SEE IT Every edge reports at two ends The graph has five edges. Its four vertices report degrees 3, 2, 3 and 2, totalling ten because each edge meets two vertices. In a network where every edge joins two vertices, adding all vertex degrees counts each edge twice. The degree of a vertex is the number of edges meeting it. Thus the degree total equals twice the edge count. The same reasoning explains why the degree total is even. An odd total is impossible, regardless of how many different drawings have been tried. For a solid assembled from faces, adding the face-edge counts may count shared edges twice. For a row of joined objects, a new object may share part of the previous boundary. A074 and A096 reward tracking which pieces are genuinely new. The useful count is determined by the joining rule, not by multiplying the size of one separate object by the number of objects. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Give each component its contribution
items.chapter: Count the same structure from two directions
items.transcript: This section is called Give each component its contribution. Suppose several measurements each include some of the same unknown quantities. Adding the measurements can be useful if every unknown appears equally often. Then the sum is a fixed multiple of the desired total. If one unknown appears more often, the extra contribution must be kept rather than silently discarded. A076 and A132 develop these related forms of bookkeeping. SEE IT A table reveals the repeated copies A 1 records one appearance of that component in the column’s pair total; a 0 records none. Each row totals two, so adding the three measurements doubles a+b+c. A contribution table can organise the argument without introducing many equations. Put one underlying component in each row and record how often it appears in each measurement. The row total tells you its coefficient in the combined sum. This explains why a particular addition or subtraction isolates the requested quantity. It also helps you notice when a visually central component is counted more often than an outer one. The same method works with two overlapping sets. An object in one set contributes once to the sum of set sizes; an object in two sets contributes twice. Subtracting the overlap once counts each object in the union once. If you want objects belonging to exactly one set, the double-counted overlap must be removed twice. Always name the desired region before choosing the correction. Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. items.title: Turn contribution limits into a sharp bound
items.chapter: Count the same structure from two directions
items.transcript: This section is called Turn contribution limits into a sharp bound. If every proposed group uses a fixed number of pairs, and no pair may be reused, the available pairs place an upper bound on the number of groups. The argument does not require constructing the groups first. Count the resource each group consumes and compare it with the total resource available. N2.30 uses this kind of incidence budget. A bound is only half an optimization solution. It proves that exceeding a number is impossible, but does not prove that the number can be reached. After obtaining the bound, construct an arrangement and check every rule. In a group-design problem, verify that no pair is repeated; in a scheduling problem, verify that no participant has conflicting assignments. A list that looks orderly can still conceal a repeated pair. Local counting can also reveal hidden global information. Different kinds of events may distribute different total contributions, so a known grand total determines how many events of each kind occurred. N2.27 combines this observation with a further restriction on a selected group. A139 similarly rewards noticing unequal incidences before trying placements. The general habit is to count contributions first and use the resulting structure to guide the construction. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Count the same structure from two directions
items.chapter: Count the same structure from two directions
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Count the same structure from two directions. Remove the two reports at each join Four unit squares form a 2-by-2 square. Find the outside perimeter by first counting the edges of the separate tiles. Coral dashed edges lie inside the completed square. Each was counted twice in the original tile reports, and neither report belongs to the outside boundary. Work through the example 1. Four separate tiles report 4 times 4=16 unit edges. 2. After joining, there are four internal shared unit edges: two along the vertical middle line and two along the horizontal middle line. 3. Each internal edge was reported by both tiles beside it. Remove two reports at each of the four joins: 16-2 times 4=8. 4. The outside outline is a square with side 2, so its perimeter is also 4 times 2=8 units. This checks the contribution count. Answer. The outside perimeter is 8 units. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. Do not copy only the answer. items.title: Find a resource that every arrangement uses
items.chapter: Prove a limit, then build an example
items.transcript: This section is called Find a resource that every arrangement uses. For a maximum, look for something limited: available positions, pairs, edges, total weight or total sum. Show how much of that resource each selected object must use. This gives an upper bound. For a minimum, ask what every arrangement must contain or cover. The same limited resource may force at least a certain number of objects, steps or days. SEE IT A bound and the arrangement that reaches it Group positions into the four adjacent pairs (1,2), (3,4), (5,6) and (7,8). Each pair holds at most one counter. The shown four-counter arrangement also obeys the neighbour rule across pairs. For a connected shape whose boundary follows horizontal and vertical grid lines, use the smallest enclosing grid rectangle, of width w and height h. The area is at most wh. The boundary contains at least 2w of horizontal segments and at least 2h of vertical segments, so its perimeter is at least 2(w+h). This perimeter argument depends on the grid-aligned edges; it does not apply unchanged to curved or diagonal boundaries. A028 is useful for distinguishing this bound from an actual arrangement that meets the tiling rules. Use all restrictions that can tighten the bound. A rough count may allow an extreme value that parity or distinctness later forbids. N1.30 develops this idea: a first counting bound is only a starting point, and a second kind of information can exclude equality. Do not discard a rough bound because it is not sharp immediately. It may reduce the problem to one critical case. Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. items.title: Explain why a promising choice is best
items.chapter: Prove a limit, then build an example
items.transcript: This section is called Explain why a promising choice is best. When a fixed total is split into positive parts, balanced parts often give a larger product. For two parts with sum S, the product can be written S squared/4-(x-S/2) squared. The squared term is nonnegative, so moving x closer to the midpoint increases the product. This explains the tendency; it is not just a pattern seen in a few calculations. SEE IT Balancing the sides increases the product These are all positive integer side-length pairs with sum 6, up to exchanging the sides. Each rectangle has perimeter 12, while its area rises from 5 to 8 to 9 as the sides become closer. Restrictions may prevent perfect balance. The parts may need to be whole numbers, distinct, or drawn from a specified set. Then find the most balanced permitted choices and prove that no other legal choice gives a better value. With more parts, an exchange argument can help: if transferring a little from an overly large part to a smaller one improves the product while preserving legality, the original arrangement was not optimal. Place-value problems use a different comparison. A digit moved to a more valuable position can outweigh all later changes, but leading-zero restrictions must be preserved. An exchange proof must describe a legal swap, not an ideal rearrangement that leaves the allowed set. A084 and A134 are useful for checking the boundary cases where a seemingly obvious greedy choice needs more careful justification. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Make equality conditions guide the construction
items.chapter: Prove a limit, then build an example
items.transcript: This section is called Make equality conditions guide the construction. After deriving a bound, inspect the places where equality would be needed. If the proof says that each day can hold at most a certain number of disjoint activities, a minimum schedule must use that capacity efficiently. If a local restriction forbids connections within a group, try placing the remaining connections between groups. N1.29 illustrates how the proof can suggest the attaining arrangement. Check the construction independently. Verify every original requirement, not just the numerical total. A candidate might reach the bound while repeating a forbidden pair, overlapping pieces, using a value twice or violating a strict inequality. Record the checks in an organised way so that the reader can see why the witness is legal. An attractive picture or a long list does not certify itself. Sometimes the correct conclusion is that the first bound cannot be attained. Then explain the obstruction and seek the next possible value. For a largest impossible total, reverse the usual task: prove one value impossible and construct every larger value. N3.29 uses a finite set of starting constructions together with a repeatable extension. That final extension is what turns a finite check into a statement about an unlimited range. items.title: Prove a limit, then build an example
items.chapter: Prove a limit, then build an example
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Prove a limit, then build an example. Use the tighter capacity bound Pack 7 red counters and 4 blue counters into trays. A tray holds at most 4 counters in total, and at most 2 of them may be red. What is the smallest possible number of trays? Empty circles are unused capacity. Leaving some spaces empty is necessary because red capacity, rather than total capacity, gives the decisive bound. Work through the example 1. There are 11 counters altogether. Since one tray holds at most 4, at least 3 trays are needed. This is only a first bound. 2. The red counters give a stronger bound: three trays can hold at most 3 times 2=6 red counters. There are 7 red counters, so at least 4 trays are necessary. 3. Use the four trays shown: RRBB, RRB, RRB and R. They contain 7 red and 4 blue counters. 4. The tray sizes are 4, 3, 3 and 1, all at most 4. Their red counts are 2, 2, 2 and 1, all at most 2. The construction meets every rule and reaches the lower bound. Answer. Exactly 4 trays are needed. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. Do not copy only the answer. Write the observation that made each next step possible, then compare your explanation with the worked example.

items.title: Build an honest sample space
items.chapter: Let the experiment determine the probability
items.transcript: This section is called Build an honest sample space. A sample space is the collection of possible complete outcomes. For equally likely outcomes, the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the number of all outcomes. Equal likelihood is an assumption to justify from the experiment. Two colour names are not automatically equally likely just because there are two names. SEE IT Colours can collect different numbers of outcomes R₁, R₂ and B₁ label three physical counters. Each has probability 1/3, but red collects two of those equal possibilities. Labelling individual objects can reveal the true outcomes. If a bag contains a red counters and b blue counters, a uniform choice gives each individual counter probability 1/(a+b). The colour red then collects a of those equal possibilities, giving probability a/(a+b). Different colours may collect different numbers of individual outcomes. The labels help the reasoning even when they are not printed on the actual counters. Choosing a bag first can change the weights. If bags have different sizes, an equally likely bag choice does not make every counter equally likely. A counter in a smaller chosen bag receives a larger share of that bag's probability. Keep both stages in the description. Pooling the objects is a different experiment unless the bag probabilities have been chosen to give every individual object the same overall chance. items.title: Track how one choice changes the next
items.chapter: Let the experiment determine the probability
items.transcript: This section is called Track how one choice changes the next. For successive choices, an ordered outcome records what happened first and what happened next. Along one route, multiply the probability of the first event by the probability of the second event given that first event. Add routes only when they are disjoint: a single completed experiment cannot follow two different complete routes at once. This is the reasoning behind a probability tree. SEE IT Update the bag before following the next branch At each draw, every remaining counter is equally likely. After red is drawn, one red and one blue remain. After blue is drawn, both remaining counters are red. Multiply along each complete route; the route probabilities sum to 1. Without replacement, the available collection changes. After a specified colour is removed, both its count and the total count may change. Write the updated composition before calculating the second probability. With replacement and a fresh uniform selection, the original composition is restored. The second choice then has the same colour probabilities regardless of the first. The wording of the selection process decides which model applies. An unordered pair can also be a useful outcome when the final event ignores order. But the numerator and denominator must use the same kind of object. Counting favourable unordered pairs and dividing by all ordered draws mixes two sample spaces. A check is to convert the entire calculation to the other model and confirm that the fraction agrees, explaining how many orders correspond to each unordered pair. items.title: Recount within the information you are given
items.chapter: Let the experiment determine the probability
items.transcript: This section is called Recount within the information you are given. A conditional probability asks for a chance after some information is known. Imagine crossing out every outcome inconsistent with that information. The remaining outcomes form the new comparison group. If the original outcomes were equally likely, the conditional probability is the favourable surviving count divided by the total surviving count. The denominator is no longer the size of the original sample space. If outcomes have unequal weights, crossing out is still a useful picture, but counts alone are insufficient. Add the probabilities of the surviving outcomes and compare the favourable surviving probability with that total. In symbols, P(E given F)=P(E and F)/P(F), provided P(F)>0. The denominator rescales the surviving group so that its total probability becomes one. This explains the formula rather than presenting it as a rule to memorise. N2.28 is a place to distinguish an object's colour from its physical identity and to keep a full record of the choices. Labelled histories can make the condition precise. After solving, check whether every favourable history satisfies the stated information. Also check the final request: a contest may ask for a quantity formed from a simplified fraction, rather than for the fraction itself. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Let the experiment determine the probability
items.chapter: Let the experiment determine the probability
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Let the experiment determine the probability. Shrink the comparison group Two fair coins are flipped independently. You are told that at least one of the coins is heads. What is the probability that both are heads? Crossing out TT changes the comparison group from four outcomes to three. HT and TH stay separate because the coins have distinct positions. Work through the example 1. Record the first coin and second coin separately. The four complete outcomes HH, HT, TH and TT each have probability 1/4. 2. The information “at least one is heads” removes TT and keeps HH, HT and TH. 3. The three surviving outcomes are still equally likely. Only HH has both coins heads. 4. Use the surviving group as the denominator: 1 favourable outcome out of 3 surviving outcomes gives probability 1/3. Answer. The conditional probability is 1/3. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. Do not copy only the answer. items.title: Keep the whole visible
items.chapter: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
items.transcript: This section is called Keep the whole visible. A fraction describes a number of equal parts relative to a chosen whole. Before using it, name that whole. A fraction of an original amount and the same fraction of a remainder usually describe different quantities. Successive changes should be recorded as multipliers acting on the current amount. An increase and a decrease by matching percentage labels therefore need not cancel. SEE IT An overlap shows a fraction of a fraction Select three of the four columns, then take two of the three rows of that selection. The purple overlap contains six of the rectangle’s twelve equal cells. To add fractions, express them using equal-sized parts. A common denominator provides that shared unit; it does not change the quantities being added. To multiply fractions, multiply the corresponding scale factors. To divide by a nonzero fraction, ask what starting quantity would produce the known result when multiplied by that fraction. This connection with inverse operations gives meaning to multiplying by the reciprocal. A fraction of a fraction is a product of scale factors, while a difference of fractions of the same whole can reveal the whole. In A017, identify which changes refer to one fixed capacity before setting up the calculation. In A094, equal fractional parts create a relationship between two different group sizes. The fractions may be equal amounts without being equal fractions of the same-sized whole. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Read decimal places as divisibility conditions
items.chapter: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
items.transcript: This section is called Read decimal places as divisibility conditions. A terminating decimal with at most k places is an integer divided by 10k. Therefore multiplying it by 10k gives an integer. This is a useful test because it turns a statement about written digits into a divisibility condition. Leading zeros after the decimal point still occupy places; trailing zeros can be removed without changing the value. SEE IT Build a power of ten from prime partners Forty supplies three 2s but only one 5. Two additional 5s pair with the unpaired 2s, making three factors of 10. Multiply the numerator by the same 25 to preserve the fraction. In lowest terms, a fraction terminates exactly when its denominator contains no primes except two and five. Every power of ten is built from those primes. If the reduced denominator has only those factors, multiplying by enough missing copies turns it into a power of ten. If another prime remains, no power of ten can supply it. Cancellation must happen before applying this test. For a positive integer k, exactly k decimal places means at most k places but not at most k-1 places after unnecessary trailing zeros are removed. N4.27 develops this distinction. It is often cleaner to count the broader divisibility condition and subtract the smaller one. For decimal shifts, track the place-value multiplier instead of moving a written point without explanation. A119 rewards interpreting the change as an exact fraction of the shifted quantity. items.title: Transform equations without losing conditions
items.chapter: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
items.transcript: This section is called Transform equations without losing conditions. An equation states that two expressions have the same value. Adding the same quantity to both sides preserves that equality. Multiplying both sides by the same nonzero quantity also preserves it and can clear denominators. Before dividing by an expression containing a variable, check that it cannot be zero; otherwise you may remove a possible case or use an invalid step. Choose transformations that reveal structure. A product condition invites factorisation, while several weighted sums may invite addition or subtraction. Expanding (x-a)(y-b) gives xy-bx-ay+ab. Reading that identity backwards shows how a combination of a product and two linear terms might become a factor-pair problem after adding the right constant. N2.29 is a place to connect an algebraic transformation with a finite, organised count. Keep the domain visible throughout: positive integers, digits, lengths or unrestricted numbers are different allowed sets. Algebra may produce a value that violates one of those meanings. A062 and A088 require bounds on digits as well as equations. After finding candidates, substitute them into the original relationship and check every domain restriction. Reversible algebra explains why none were lost; the final checks explain why the survivors are valid. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
items.chapter: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree. Solve the equality shown by the bars Three identical trays each hold one pouch and 2 loose counters. Every pouch contains the same number of counters. The three trays contain 21 counters altogether. How many counters are in each pouch? The top bar separates the total into three equal trays. The lower bar separates one tray’s seven counters into a pouch and two loose counters. Work through the example 1. Let x be the non-negative whole number of counters in one pouch. Each tray holds x+2 counters, so 3(x+2)=21. 2. The three equal tray totals share the 21 counters equally. Divide both sides by 3: x+2=7. 3. Remove the 2 loose counters from each tray total: x=7-2=5. 4. Check the original story: each tray has 5+2=7 counters, and three trays have 3 times 7=21. The answer is a permitted whole-number count. Answer. Each pouch contains 5 counters. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. Do not copy only the answer. Write the observation that made each next step possible, then compare your explanation with the worked example.

items.title: Build a recurrence from a reversible step
items.chapter: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
items.transcript: This section is called Build a recurrence from a reversible step. A recurrence expresses a new value using earlier values. For a route-counting problem, group routes by their last move. Remove that move and identify the smaller problem left behind. The groups must be disjoint, and every legal route must belong to one. Conversely, each allowed shorter route must extend in the stated way. This reversible connection is the proof behind the recurrence. SEE IT The final tile gives two complete cases F(n) counts tilings of an n-cell strip using 1-cell and 2-cell tiles. Each tiling ends in exactly one of these two ways; removing or restoring the final tile gives a reversible match. The starting values are F(0) = 1 for the empty strip and F(1) = 1. Starting values are part of the rule. There is one empty sequence of moves, even though it contains no moves. That single starting object allows a first move to be appended once. Counts at unreachable negative positions are zero. These conventions are not tricks: they describe actual possible and impossible histories. A040 and A081 are useful for seeing how a changed set of permitted moves changes the recurrence. Do not import a familiar sequence because the first few entries look similar. Different rules can agree for several early cases and then separate. Calculate small cases from the definition, explain the transition, and only then build a table. Check a later table entry by a different classification if possible. An agreement between two independently justified methods is more informative than extending one guessed pattern twice. Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. Then draw the smallest model, table or example that would help you recognise the same idea in a new problem.

items.title: Remember enough information, but no more
items.chapter: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
items.transcript: This section is called Remember enough information, but no more. A location alone may not determine the legal next move. If a rule depends on the previous move, the state must remember that move as well. If a route may not revisit a place, it may need to remember which places have already been visited. Combining histories that allow different futures can create illegal routes or lose legal ones. SEE IT Mark the first complete repeated state The state is the current remainder. Starting at 0, four steps return to 0, so the same four-state cycle repeats. Each arrow label gives the new total and the remainder it leaves on division by 5. Once the state is adequate, histories with that same state can share a count. Update each state from the states that can lead into it, and keep the conditions on each transition visible. A053 uses a restricted running difference; A123 and A143 use repeated numerical rules. The information needed for these processes is different, even though each can be organised by states. For a deterministic process, repeating the full state forces the same future, because the next state is determined by the current one. Repeating just one visible feature may not. If the process continues indefinitely and only finitely many states are possible, some state must eventually repeat, giving an initial nonrepeating segment followed by a cycle. Mark those two parts separately when finding a distant term. The target position must be measured from the actual cycle start. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Classify game positions by their legal moves
items.chapter: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
items.transcript: This section is called Classify game positions by their legal moves. In a finite take-away game, call a position winning if the player about to move can force a win against every response. Call it losing if that player cannot. For the usual rule that taking the last object wins, the empty position is losing for the player who would move next: the previous move has already ended the game. A position is winning if at least one legal move leads to a losing position. It is losing if every legal move leads to a winning position. These statements describe perfect play, not a prediction about what an inexperienced opponent might choose. Build the smallest positions first, because each larger position depends only on smaller ones. N3.26 is a place to turn this classification into a strategy. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
items.chapter: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Build patterns from reasons, not guesses. Explain an L-shaped addition A square array of dots grows from 3 rows of 3 to 4 rows of 4. How many dots are added? Explain a rule for growing any n-by-n square to the next square, where n is a positive whole number. The coral row owns the corner dot. The purple part contains only the remaining column, so the two additions do not overlap. Work through the example 1. Keep all 9 original dots. Add a bottom row of 4 dots. 2. The new right-hand column still needs 3 dots above that row. Do not count the bottom-right corner twice. 3. The addition is 4 + 3 = 7, so the next square has 9 + 7 = 16 dots. 4. For an n-by-n square, the new row has n + 1 dots and the rest of the new column has n dots. The increase is 2n + 1. This construction explains why consecutive square numbers differ by successive odd numbers. Answer. 7 dots are added; in general the increase is 2n + 1. items.title: Translate position into value
items.chapter: Make every digit obey both its jobs
items.transcript: This section is called Translate position into value. A two-digit number with tens digit a and units digit b is 10a+b. A three-digit number is 100a+10b+c. The leading digit must be nonzero, while later digits may be zero unless the question forbids it. Write these allowed ranges beside the expression. A letter representing a digit is not an unrestricted algebraic unknown. SEE IT A digit’s position supplies its multiplier Each long rod is ten units. Swapping 4 and 2 preserves the digit sum 6, but changes 42 into 24: their difference is 18. Reversal can create useful cancellation because corresponding place values exchange. Repetition can create a different simplification: a palindrome fixes some positions to be equal. But similar-looking patterns must still be translated from their own definitions. A055, A071 and A088 require different relationships between the positions. Start with the full value expression, then simplify; do not replace it by a rule remembered from another digit puzzle. In a cryptarithm, use carries as extra constraints. The units column restricts the next carry, which restricts the tens column, and so on. A carry is a small whole number determined by the size of the column total. An equation that fits the written last digit may still have the wrong carry. A129 is useful for checking each column and then verifying the completed multiplication as a whole. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Use information that survives rearrangement
items.chapter: Make every digit obey both its jobs
items.transcript: This section is called Use information that survives rearrangement. Because ten leaves remainder one on division by nine, every power of ten does too. A number therefore has the same remainder modulo nine as the sum of its digits. The corresponding divisibility-by-three rule follows for the same reason. Rearranging digits preserves their sum, so it preserves these remainder tests even though it usually changes the value. SEE IT Each place contributes one remainder per digit unit The purple cell is the extra one in each place-value unit. Removing multiples of 9 leaves the digit sum; that sum may still contain another group of 9. Other divisibility rules depend on position. Divisibility by four depends on the final two digits because the contribution from all earlier places is a multiple of one hundred, and hence a multiple of four. Evenness depends only on the units digit. Combining a digit-sum test with an ending restriction can be much more effective than either alone. A100 and A108 are places to keep both kinds of information active. Bounds often turn a remainder condition into an exact sum. If the allowed digits constrain a total to a short interval, perhaps only one multiple of the required divisor lies there. State the bounds and explain why they hold. A digit-product condition can be handled through prime factors instead; a zero digit makes the product zero, so positivity of the product can rule it out immediately. items.title: Organise counts, inventories and next-number
items.chapter: Make every digit obey both its jobs
items.transcript: This section is called Organise counts, inventories and next-number. searches Decide whether you are counting numbers, positions or occurrences. For an occurrence count, examine each place separately and add the contributions. A number with repeated copies of a digit then correctly contributes more than once. A043, A089 and A140 develop different forms of place-by-place bookkeeping. When counting numbers containing a digit, a complement may instead avoid repeated counting. For a digit inventory, compare requirements with the stock of each symbol. A surplus of one digit does not automatically repair a shortage of another. Treat interchangeable orientations together only when the question explicitly permits the same physical mark to serve both roles. A036 rewards this distinction between written values and available pieces. The permitted physical operation is part of the mathematics. For ordinary positive integers, first compare the number of digits. Among numerals of the same length, the first differing digit decides which number is larger. To find the next larger valid number of a fixed length, preserve the longest prefix that can still be completed as a larger valid number, increase the next digit by the smallest amount that permits a valid completion, and use the smallest legal suffix. Extra restrictions can make a sorted suffix invalid. A120 and A145 require careful control of the permitted digits and their positions. Watch out for these • A leading zero shortens a numeral; a code may permit it, but an ordinary fixed-length number does not. • Divisibility by three or nine survives permutation, while an ending-based divisibility test may change. • When counting printed digits, repeated occurrences count separately; when counting qualifying numbers, each number counts once. Carry this idea forward Keep place value, digit restrictions and counting conventions separate until they can be combined precisely. Each surviving candidate must satisfy all three kinds of condition. Ready to try it? items.title: Make every digit obey both its jobs
items.chapter: Make every digit obey both its jobs
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Make every digit obey both its jobs. Follow both carries Add 58 and 67. Explain what each carry means, and why the answer has a hundreds digit. The purple arrow carries one ten from the ones column. The coral arrow carries one hundred from the tens column. Work through the example 1. In the ones column, 8 + 7 = 15 ones. Regroup 10 ones as 1 ten, leaving 5 ones. 2. In the tens column, the original 5 tens and 6 tens join the carried ten: 5 + 6 + 1 = 12 tens. 3. Regroup 10 tens as 1 hundred, leaving 2 tens. The answer is 1 hundred, 2 tens and 5 ones. 4. Check the value directly: 50 + 60 + 8 + 7 = 110 + 15 = 125. Each regrouping kept the total unchanged. Answer. 58 + 67 = 125. items.title: Build an angle chain from dependable facts
items.chapter: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts
items.transcript: This section is called Build an angle chain from dependable facts. Angles around a point total a full turn of 360 degrees, and angles on a straight line total a half turn of 180 degrees. An acute angle is greater than 0 degrees and smaller than 90 degrees, a right angle equals 90 degrees, and an obtuse angle is larger than 90 degrees but smaller than 180 degrees. Vertically opposite angles are equal because each is the supplement of the same adjacent angle. Parallel lines create equal corresponding and alternate angles when crossed by a transversal. Identify which line directions form each angle before using one of these relationships. SEE IT A triangle’s angle sum becomes visible The added line passes through the top vertex and is parallel to the base. Alternate angles transfer α and β to the top; together with γ they make 180 degrees. A triangle's interior angles total half a turn. One way to see this is to draw through a vertex a line parallel to the opposite side: the other two triangle angles appear beside the vertex angle along that straight line. Equal sides in an isosceles triangle give equal opposite angles. These facts can be chained, but every step must refer to the correct triangle or pair of lines. For a convex polygon, diagonals from one vertex split it into triangles without overlap. Counting those triangles gives the interior-angle sum. A regular polygon also has equal angles and equal sides, which supplies more information than the angle sum alone. Do not use regularity merely because a drawing looks balanced. A016 is a useful place to distinguish what follows from equal-sided components from what only appears visually symmetrical. Before moving on, open your notebook.
