items.title: Connect angles on a circle to the arcs they see
items.chapter: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts
items.transcript: This section is called Connect angles on a circle to the arcs they see. An arc is a portion of a circle's circumference between two points. Its measure is the central angle swept out along that arc; for a major arc this is a reflex angle greater than 180 degrees. Equal spacing around a circle gives equal central angles, so the size of an arc can be found by counting equal gaps. Count the gaps along the relevant arc, not the number of points encountered including both ends. SEE IT Use the arc that does not contain the viewing vertex Both angles use endpoints A and C. The coral arc is 120 degrees around the centre, so the inscribed angle at B is 60 degrees. The other arc contains B and is not the arc used here. For three distinct points A, B and C on a circle, angle ABC is half the measure of the arc AC that does not contain B. To prove this, let O be the centre and D the point diametrically opposite B. For a point P equal to A or C, but different from D, write α = angle PBD. The equal radii OB and OP make triangle BOP isosceles, so angle BOP = 180 degrees - 2α. Since OB and OD point in opposite directions, the arc PD avoiding B has measure 180 degrees - angle BOP = 2α. If A and C lie on opposite sides of diameter BD, add the two angles at B and the two arcs through D. If they lie on the same side, take the absolute difference of the two angles and of the two arcs. In either case, the arc AC avoiding B has twice the measure of angle ABC. If A or C equals D, its angle and arc contribution are zero, so the same calculation still applies. The choice of arc is essential. The same two endpoints determine two arcs, and only the one not containing the viewing vertex belongs to that angle. For a triangle with all vertices on a circle, the three gaps between successive chosen vertices control its three angles. N4.30 connects this fact with a complete counting argument. A strict inequality must remain strict when translated from angle size to arc size. Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. Then draw the smallest model, table or example that would help you recognise the same idea in a new problem.

items.title: Use coordinates or extra lines to make a proof visible
items.chapter: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts
items.transcript: This section is called Use coordinates or extra lines to make a proof visible. An auxiliary line is a line added to your working because it exposes a known relationship. It may produce a perpendicular height, an isosceles triangle or two triangles with a shared base. Explain why the line helps before calculating. Adding many unrelated lines can make a diagram harder to read without creating any usable information. Coordinates offer another exact representation. Choose axes that match existing horizontal or vertical structure, then describe points by their positions. Differences of coordinates describe movement between points. Equal coordinate changes can establish parallel directions; fixed horizontal or vertical lines reveal perpendicular distances. The coordinates are a model of the stated geometry, so choosing them must not introduce an unproved midpoint, equality or right angle. For any points X, P and Y, the triangle inequality says XP + PY ≥ XY. Equality holds exactly when P lies on the straight segment from X to Y. Three positive lengths form a nondegenerate triangle exactly when each is shorter than the sum of the other two; for lengths ordered a ≤ b ≤ c, it is enough to check a + b > c. A reflection preserves distances, and every point on its mirror line stays fixed. Reflecting one endpoint can therefore turn a shortest broken route through a line into a straight-segment problem. Lattice diagrams require an additional distinction: a segment may pass through grid points between its endpoints. A059 is a place to examine that structure instead of counting only visible endpoint pairs. Whether using coordinates, angle chasing or a construction, finish by relating the derived quantity to the requested one. A proof should explain why changing the drawing while preserving the facts would leave the conclusion unchanged. Watch out for these • Do not infer a midpoint, a right angle or equal lengths from appearance alone. • For a circle angle, use the arc opposite its vertex; the other arc gives a different relationship. • Angles strictly below a threshold must not be mixed with angles equal to that threshold when counting cases. Carry this idea forward Use a small chain of justified geometric facts. A diagram suggests where to look; angle relationships, stated equalities and exact coordinates establish what is true. Ready to try it? A016, A059, N4.30, K011 Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. Then draw the smallest model, table or example that would help you recognise the same idea in a new problem.

items.title: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts
items.chapter: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts. The angle outside a triangle Triangle ABC has angle A = 48 degrees and angle B = 67 degrees. Extend BC beyond C to D. Find angle ACD and check it using the two other triangle angles. The teal 65 degrees is inside the triangle. The purple 115 degrees is outside, between CA and the extension CD. Work through the example 1. The triangle’s interior angles sum to 180 degrees, so angle ACB = 180 degrees - 48 degrees - 67 degrees = 65 degrees. 2. CB and CD point in opposite directions along one straight line. Therefore angles ACB and ACD sum to 180 degrees. 3. Angle ACD = 180 degrees - 65 degrees = 115 degrees. 4. Substitution explains a second check: 180 degrees - (180 degrees - 48 degrees - 67 degrees) = 48 degrees + 67 degrees = 115 degrees. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles. Answer. Angle ACD = 115 degrees. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. items.title: Use bases, heights and complementary regions
items.chapter: Measure the region or solid that matters
items.transcript: This section is called Use bases, heights and complementary regions. A triangle has area bh/2, where b is the chosen base and h is its perpendicular height. Two congruent copies can form a parallelogram with base b and height h, explaining the factor of one half. A sloping side is usually not the height. If a vertex moves along a line parallel to the base, the perpendicular height stays fixed, so the area stays fixed too. SEE IT Area depends on perpendicular height The two triangles share the same base. Their top vertices lie on a parallel line 3 cm above it, so sliding the vertex changes the shape but leaves the area at 9 cm squared. Triangles with a common height have areas in the same ratio as their bases. Triangles with a common base have areas in the same ratio as their perpendicular heights. These comparisons can avoid finding either area separately. An unknown height may also disappear when two distances add to a known total. A047 and A152 reward choosing useful bases and heights before attempting to measure sloping edges. When a shaded region is awkward, calculate its complement inside an easier whole. A018 is a place to organise the outside pieces and check that they neither overlap nor leave gaps. If regions do overlap, adding their areas counts the intersection more than once. Use the contribution reasoning from Chapter T06 to correct the total. The same arithmetic can describe a union or an exactly-one region, but the required correction differs. items.title: Separate boundary change from scale change
items.chapter: Measure the region or solid that matters
items.transcript: This section is called Separate boundary change from scale change. Perimeter counts exposed boundary length. Removing a piece removes some old boundary and may create new boundary. Compare those changes directly. A corner cut can replace horizontal and vertical lengths by equal new lengths, while a cut in the middle of an edge can create extra boundary. The removed area alone does not determine the perimeter change. Scaling every length by a factor k scales area by k squared and volume by k cubed. A rectangle's two dimensions each receive the length factor; a rectangular solid's three dimensions each receive it. These relationships explain why doubling a length factor does not merely double area or volume. They apply to similar shapes and solids, where every relevant linear dimension changes by the same factor. A volume formula must match the solid. A prism with constant cross-sectional area A and height h has volume Ah because equal-thickness slices have equal volume. For a submerged object's effect on a water level, the tank's cross-section at that level matters. A rectangular base by itself does not guarantee vertical sides. Keep assumptions such as full submersion, constant cross-section and no overflow explicit when using a displacement model. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Count hidden pieces through layers and boundaries
items.chapter: Measure the region or solid that matters
items.transcript: This section is called Count hidden pieces through layers and boundaries. A drawing of a solid shows only some of its pieces. Decide whether the solid is filled, hollow, layered or merely a framework. A060, A087 and A106 use different layer descriptions. Find the number of pieces in one exact layer or slice, then explain how those slices cover the entire solid once. Visible squares on the outside do not directly count interior cubes. SEE IT Hidden cubes belong to a layer too A layer has 3  times  2 = 6 cubes. There are 2 layers, including the lower cubes hidden by the upper layer in the oblique view, so the solid contains 12 cubes. For painted-cube questions, classify a small cube by which boundary faces it touches. Corners, edge interiors, face interiors and the interior of the block have different numbers of exposed faces. If one large face is unpainted, the classification changes at that face. Counting unpainted cubes first can be easier, but any shortcut must respect small dimensions where an assumed interior row does not exist. For tunnels or removed portions, identify intersections before adding volumes. A cube lying in several tunnels must be removed only once. With three overlapping sets, subtracting all pairwise intersections removes their common intersection too many times, so its contribution must be restored appropriately. A037 develops this bookkeeping. For a net such as A127, first determine which drawn lengths correspond to the same solid dimension, then calculate volume from the recovered dimensions. Watch out for these • A triangle height is perpendicular to the chosen base; it is not simply a nearby sloping edge. • A perimeter is the boundary that remains exposed, not the sum of boundaries of separated component pieces. • Do not count only visible cubes when the stated solid is filled. Explain a layer or coordinate classification that includes the hidden ones. Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. Then draw the smallest model, table or example that would help you recognise the same idea in a new problem.

items.title: Measure the region or solid that matters
items.chapter: Measure the region or solid that matters
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Measure the region or solid that matters. A cut changes the boundary Start with two rectangles, each 6 cm by 4 cm. Remove a 1 cm by 1 cm square from a corner of one rectangle, and a 1 cm by 1 cm square from the middle of an edge of the other. What are the two new perimeters? Dashed grey segments are removed boundary. Coral segments are new exposed boundary. The unlabelled notch sides are all 1 cm. Work through the example 1. Each original perimeter is 2  times  (6 + 4) = 20 cm. 2. The corner cut removes two old 1 cm boundary segments and exposes two new 1 cm segments. Its change is -2 + 2 = 0 cm. 3. The edge notch removes one old 1 cm boundary segment and exposes three new 1 cm segments. Its change is -1 + 3 = 2 cm. 4. The new perimeters are therefore 20 cm and 22 cm. Both remaining areas are 24 - 1 = 23 cm squared, which shows why removed area alone cannot determine a perimeter change. Answer. Corner cut: 20 cm. Edge notch: 22 cm. items.title: Translate the movement rules exactly
items.chapter: Turn routes and schedules into networks
items.transcript: This section is called Translate the movement rules exactly. Two drawn lines crossing do not necessarily create a meeting point. A connection exists only when the problem's rules or markings establish one. Likewise, touching at a corner may or may not permit a move. Read the definition of adjacency before counting. A013 and A109 use different kinds of local connection, so their permitted moves must be read from their own diagrams. SEE IT The last edge separates routes into cases Each circle shows the number of directed routes from S. Only the drawn arrows are permitted. A route arriving at T comes from C or D, giving 2 + 3 = 5. Record direction if movement is restricted. An undirected edge permits movement both ways; a directed edge permits only the stated direction. Also record whether a route may revisit a vertex, reuse an edge, or pass through every vertex exactly once. These are different problems. A sequence that obeys adjacency can still be illegal because it repeats a forbidden location. For a route that only moves forward through an ordered network, count paths into each vertex by adding the counts from its legal predecessors. Every route into the vertex has a unique last edge, so the predecessor cases are disjoint and complete. Start with one empty route at the starting vertex. Give blocked or unreachable vertices count zero. A138 is useful for checking this rule one location at a time. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Use future obligations to reject tempting moves
items.chapter: Turn routes and schedules into networks
items.transcript: This section is called Use future obligations to reject tempting moves. When a route must visit many locations without repetition, a locally legal move may make the final goal impossible. After a proposed move, inspect what remains. Can every unvisited location still be reached? Has a location become cut off? Does a branch have only one usable connection left, forcing it to be an endpoint? These are necessary conditions that can eliminate choices early. SEE IT A local obligation can prove impossibility To visit all four vertices exactly once, each degree-one vertex would have to be an endpoint. There are three such vertices, but a path has only two endpoints, so no route works. A route required to visit every vertex exactly once is often called a Hamiltonian path. The name does not supply a formula. The useful reasoning comes from the particular network: narrow passages, dead ends, forced neighbours and separations. A128 and A144 reward explaining why certain continuations must occur, rather than merely presenting one route that happens to work. For a maximum-value route, compare all required omissions with an explicit successful route. For a largest code, examine possible next symbols in descending order but reject a symbol only with a reason that no valid completion exists. A103 combines a route construction with an upper bound on what can be collected. The construction shows possibility; the argument about unavoidable omissions establishes optimality. Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. Then draw the smallest model, table or example that would help you recognise the same idea in a new problem.

items.title: Read a schedule as groups of nonconflicting edges
items.chapter: Turn routes and schedules into networks
items.transcript: This section is called Read a schedule as groups of nonconflicting edges. A schedule can also be represented by a network. Participants are vertices and required meetings are edges. If a participant can take part in at most one meeting during a time slot, the edges placed in that slot must have no shared vertex. This turns a verbal conflict rule into a precise structural condition. Count the total required meetings and the maximum number that can fit in one slot. Dividing gives a lower bound on the number of slots, rounded up if necessary. Individual participants can create another lower bound through their own number of required meetings. Use the strongest available bound, but remember that capacity alone does not guarantee a conflict-free schedule. All the required edges must still be placed legally. N4.29 shows why capacity is only a first bound. Its rest-day restriction and the odd number of participants rule out shorter schedules. The attaining schedule must satisfy the rest pattern as well as use every required pair exactly once and avoid conflicts within each day. Rotation or modular labelling can help organise pairings, but the arrangement must also meet every restriction linking consecutive time slots. Verify these properties separately. A042 adds timing conditions to movement rather than pairwise meetings; there the repeating time structure must be read alongside the distance and speed restrictions. items.title: Turn routes and schedules into networks
items.chapter: Turn routes and schedules into networks
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Turn routes and schedules into networks. Schedule only the required meetings Five pupils A, B, C, D and E need only these meetings: AB, AC, AD, BE and CE. A pupil can attend at most one meeting in a time slot. Find the smallest possible number of slots and give a schedule. Each column is one set of nonconflicting edges. The busiest pupil gives a lower bound; the three columns show that the bound can be reached. Work through the example 1. A has to meet B, C and D. Those three meetings cannot share a slot, so at least 3 slots are necessary. 2. In slot 1, hold AB and CE. These meetings involve four different pupils. 3. In slot 2, hold AC and BE. Again the two meetings have no pupil in common. 4. In slot 3, hold AD. The list now contains each of the five required pairs once, with no other meeting needed. 5. The lower bound of 3 slots is attained by this schedule, so it is the minimum. Answer. 3 slots: AB with CE; AC with BE; then AD. items.title: Define sameness before counting
items.chapter: Use symmetry without losing or repeating cases
items.transcript: This section is called Define sameness before counting. A rotation moves a figure by turning it. A reflection reverses its orientation as a mirror would. A physical solid can be rotated in space, but a mirror image is not always obtainable by a rotation. Similarly, exchanging colour names may preserve some properties while creating a different colouring under the question's rules. Never add an equivalence that the problem has not allowed. SEE IT A turn and a mirror change different things The coloured labels are fixed identities. A rotation keeps their clockwise order. Reflection reverses that order, so this reflected labelled triangle cannot be obtained by a rotation alone. Distinguish an arrangement of pieces from its outside outline. Different internal joins can sometimes produce the same outline. If only outlines count, those constructions belong to one outcome; if placements of individual pieces count, they may be different. A041 and A082 reward a careful reading of the allowed joins and the meaning of “different” before the pictures are classified. One way to compare two candidates is to move each through every permitted orientation and choose a standard description, such as the smallest coordinate or label pattern. Matching standard descriptions identifies the same class. This method is useful for checking a finite list, but the description must preserve all relevant information: colours, incidences, piece boundaries and any labels that the question distinguishes. items.title: Do not divide by a symmetry count blindly
items.chapter: Use symmetry without losing or repeating cases
items.transcript: This section is called Do not divide by a symmetry count blindly. A symmetry may leave some objects unchanged. Such an object has fewer visibly different orientations than an object with no symmetry. Therefore dividing a raw count by the number of rotations can fail: not every outcome has been counted that many times. Establish equal repetition before using division, just as in ordinary unordered counting. SEE IT Count the distinct appearances of each object Turn each marked square through 0 degrees, 90 degrees, 180 degrees and 270 degrees. The three kinds of marking give 1, 2 and 4 different appearances. Equal numbers of turns do not guarantee equal repetition. For a cube, there are six choices for the upward face and four choices for a neighbouring face to point forward, giving twenty-four rotations. But this does not mean every cube colouring has twenty-four different appearances. Some colourings look unchanged under several rotations. A026 is a place to classify colour patterns carefully instead of dividing the initial selection count by the rotation total. A useful first classification uses properties that rotations cannot change: the number of marked corners on a face, the pattern of adjacencies, or the number of components. Different values of such a property prove two objects different. Equal values do not necessarily prove them the same. You may need a finer classification or an explicit allowed motion connecting the two candidates. An invariant can separate classes without fully identifying them. items.title: Pair objects or classify their local structure
items.chapter: Use symmetry without losing or repeating cases
items.transcript: This section is called Pair objects or classify their local structure. Sometimes symmetry gives an exact pairing rather than a complicated rotation class. If an operation reverses itself when applied twice and has no fixed objects, every object is paired with a different partner. A sign reversal can pair positive and negative totals, provided no total is zero. Before halving a count, prove those conditions and prove that different constructions really give different totals. N3.28 combines these requirements. Local patterns can also produce a complete classification. Fix one allowed orientation or colour temporarily, then describe all ways the remaining parts can attach while satisfying the rules. Restore any genuinely different initial choices at the end. A068, A148 and A151 use local restrictions to constrain neighbouring cells. A rule involving every small region must be checked in every such region, not just in the most visible ones. Finally, distinguish a history from its result. Several deletions or rearrangements can collapse to one final word or shape. N3.30 asks for a classification of resulting words, so each proposed class needs a reason why its members coincide and why different classes stay different. A successful enumeration explains both uniqueness and completeness; a gallery of attractive examples provides only the existence part. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Use symmetry without losing or repeating cases
items.chapter: Use symmetry without losing or repeating cases
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Use symmetry without losing or repeating cases. Pair choices by toggling one member Choose any subset of {A, B, C}, including the empty set. Explain why exactly half of the eight subsets have an even number of members. Teal cells have even size and purple cells have odd size. The empty set ∅ participates in the pairing just like every other subset. Work through the example 1. Each of A, B and C can be chosen or not chosen, so there are 2  times  2  times  2 = 8 subsets. 2. Pair each subset with the result of toggling A: add A when it is absent, and remove A when it is present. 3. Toggling A twice returns to the starting subset. Toggling once always changes the subset, so no subset is left unpaired. 4. The size changes by exactly 1, so every pair contains one even-sized subset and one odd-sized subset. 5. There are 8  divided by  2 = 4 pairs, giving 4 even-sized subsets and 4 odd-sized subsets. The empty set has size 0, which is even. Answer. 4 of the 8 subsets have even size. items.title: Turn a ratio into equal parts
items.chapter: Keep ratios, rates and averages precise
items.transcript: This section is called Turn a ratio into equal parts. A ratio a: b means that the two quantities can be written ak and bk for one common scale k. Their total is (a+b)k and their difference is (a-b)k, with the order chosen consistently. A known quantity or total determines k when its coefficient is nonzero. A known difference determines k only when a≠b. The ratio labels are numbers of equal parts, not the quantities themselves. SEE IT Ratio labels count parts, not objects Both bars use the same-sized part. Group A gets 3 of the 5 parts, so its fraction of the whole is 3/5 and its count is 15; group B gets 10. Fractions of the whole use the total number of parts in the denominator. A ratio between two groups is different from the fraction of all members belonging to one group. When two fractional portions are equal, translate that equality before deciding which group is larger. A094 can be revisited through this lens, while A136 connects several ratio conditions through a shared whole-number scale. For linked ratios, identify the quantity shared between them and give it the same value in both representations. Simply adding ratio labels from unrelated scales is invalid. Age problems add another condition: the same elapsed time is added to everyone's age, preserving age differences but generally changing age ratios. A005 and A035 require such relationships to be combined with ordinary restrictions on order and distinctness. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Convert time descriptions into rates
items.chapter: Keep ratios, rates and averages precise
items.transcript: This section is called Convert time descriptions into rates. For a fixed job, a worker who completes it in time T has rate 1/T jobs per unit time, assuming constant work rate. Rates for simultaneous independent contributions can be added when they measure the same kind of work in the same time unit. Completion times themselves cannot generally be added or averaged to obtain the joint time. A008 and A104 reward finding a common unit of work first. SEE IT Add the two contributions to closing one gap In the same minute, A removes 6 m from the left of the gap and B removes 4 m from the right. With constant speeds they meet after 50  divided by  10 = 5 minutes. An amount produced equals rate multiplied by time. If workers have different rate ratios and work for different durations, their total contributions depend on both. A050 develops this distinction. Keep the unit attached: items per hour multiplied by hours gives items. A unit check often reveals that an attractive multiplication or division has combined the wrong quantities. For motion towards one another, the gap closes at the sum of the speeds. For motion in the same direction, the gap changes at their difference, with the sign indicating which object gains. On a circular track, a meeting may correspond to a full lap of relative motion rather than the distance one runner travels. A091 requires the motion relationship to be interpreted before a missing individual rate is recovered. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Recover totals and interpret averages
items.chapter: Keep ratios, rates and averages precise
items.transcript: This section is called Recover totals and interpret averages. For a nonempty finite list of numbers, the arithmetic mean is the sum divided by the number of entries. Find the median after sorting the entries from smallest to largest: with an odd number of entries it is the middle entry; with an even number it is the mean of the two middle entries. Repeated values still occupy separate positions. The range is the largest entry minus the smallest. These statistics describe different features, so equal means and equal ranges do not force equal medians. When a mean is given, recover the sum before combining it with other conditions. Average speed is total distance divided by total time. It is a time-weighted average of the separate speeds, because a speed maintained for longer contributes for more of the journey. Equal distances do not imply equal times. A slower leg can take much longer than a faster leg, so an ordinary mean of the speed labels may give the wrong result. The same principle applies to combined scores and prices. Recover each group's total before combining groups of unequal sizes. For a mixture price, total cost divided by total mass gives the price per unit mass. For an exchange, track the units through each conversion and reverse the rate when travelling in the opposite direction. A020 uses rates supplied within its problem; their role is to connect the currency amounts exactly. Distinguish distance travelled from net displacement. Travelling away and returning uses time and distance even when some of the displacement cancels. A118 rewards accounting for the entire route. After any rate calculation, reconstruct the quantities over the claimed time and check that they satisfy the original total or meeting condition. The check should test the story's relationship, not merely repeat the division that produced the answer. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Keep ratios, rates and averages precise
items.chapter: Keep ratios, rates and averages precise
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Keep ratios, rates and averages precise. Combine totals before averaging Two learners each score 6 points, and three learners each score 10 points. What is the mean score for all five learners? Explain why averaging 6 and 10 directly gives the wrong answer. Each dot represents one learner, including repeated scores. Three dots sit at 10, so the mean lies closer to 10 than to 6. Work through the example 1. The first group contributes 2  times  6 = 12 points. The second contributes 3  times  10 = 30 points. 2. Together they contribute 12 + 30 = 42 points across 2 + 3 = 5 learners. 3. The mean is total points divided by the number of learners: 42  divided by  5 = 8.4 points. 4. The calculation (6 + 10)  divided by  2 = 8 gives equal weight to the two groups, although their sizes are different. Each learner needs equal weight, so 10 must be counted three times and 6 twice. 5. Check: five scores averaging 8.4 have total 5  times  8.4 = 42, which matches the original total. Answer. The mean is 8.4 points. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. Do not copy only the answer. Write the observation that made each next step possible, then compare your explanation with the worked example.

items.title: Match the strength of the proof to the claim
items.chapter: Write proofs that leave no hidden cases
items.transcript: This section is called Match the strength of the proof to the claim. An example proves that something can happen. It does not prove that it always happens or that it is the only possibility. A necessary condition is one every solution must satisfy; a sufficient condition guarantees a solution. They may differ. Passing a divisibility test, for instance, can be necessary without enforcing all the other digit restrictions in a problem. SEE IT A bound becomes a maximum only when reached The area bound rules out five dominoes. The four coloured dominoes meet the rules and do not overlap, so four is both possible and optimal. For uniqueness, show that every legal solution must lie among your candidates, then show that exactly one candidate works. If your algebra consists of reversible steps, say why the allowed values remain unchanged. If a step only gives a necessary condition, return to the original problem to test the survivors. A052 and A117 are useful for examining whether every permitted position or case has really been covered. For counting, state why cases are disjoint and exhaustive. An interval and a parity restriction may describe where answers can lie without proving that every permitted value in that interval is attainable. A124 develops this gap between bounding a range and filling it. A complete solution must supply the missing construction or correspondence, rather than treating a plausible list of possibilities as established fact. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Use counterexamples and contradictions carefully
items.chapter: Write proofs that leave no hidden cases
items.transcript: This section is called Use counterexamples and contradictions carefully. To disprove a statement claiming that every object has a property, one legal counterexample is enough. The word legal matters: the example must satisfy all the statement's assumptions. An apparent exception outside the allowed set does not refute the claim. When a method fails, ask which assumption it needed; this can turn an error into a more accurate theorem. A contradiction proof begins by assuming the opposite of what you want to establish, then derives an impossibility using the problem's conditions. An odd degree total in an ordinary finite network contradicts the fact that every edge has two endpoints. A proposed equality case may contradict a parity requirement. The final sentence should identify the incompatible facts explicitly, not merely announce that the attempt “does not work”. For truth-and-lie constraints such as A002, assign each speaker a proposed status, then evaluate the exact claim being made. A truth teller's claim must be true and a liar's false. Propagate these requirements, then check every speaker for consistency before accepting an assignment. A failed construction is not a contradiction. It rules out only that construction unless you prove it represents every possibility. Organise failures by a complete classification or replace trial with an invariant, a bound or a divisibility obstruction. N1.30 demonstrates how a general obstruction can eliminate an entire proposed equality case, while A097 uses bounds to reduce a search to a small set of forced possibilities. items.title: Connect finite checks to general conclusions
items.chapter: Write proofs that leave no hidden cases
items.transcript: This section is called Connect finite checks to general conclusions. A finite exhaustive search can establish a finite claim if the search space is complete and every acceptance test matches the conditions. Explain the range, the classification and why nothing lies outside it. A computer can help verify such a search, but a list of outputs without a description of what was checked leaves the mathematical coverage unclear. SEE IT A starting block and a valid extension cover every case Every whole number at least 6 appears in exactly one lane. If a property is true at 6, 7 and 8 and is preserved by adding 3, it is true everywhere in these lanes; k is any non-negative whole number. For an unlimited family, finite checking alone is insufficient. You need a rule extending the verified cases. Induction provides one form: establish starting cases, then prove that the truth of suitable smaller cases forces the next one. A recurrence proof uses this idea when every route is obtained from shorter legal routes. N3.29 uses an extension by a fixed available increment to cover all larger values from a finite starting block. Finish by checking both the requested conclusion and its scope. Have you proved a maximum or merely an upper bound? All solutions or one? Every starting state or only the tested ones? A115 requires an attaining arrangement as well as a lower bound, and A063 requires separate treatment of cases with different multiplicities. A brief final sentence naming the completed claim helps expose any missing half of the argument. Watch out for these • One counterexample disproves an “always” claim only when it satisfies every assumption of that claim. • A necessary condition is a filter, not automatically a complete solution. Test the survivors. • A finite pattern does not prove an unlimited rule; supply a transition, invariant or extension that covers the untested cases. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Write proofs that leave no hidden cases
items.chapter: Write proofs that leave no hidden cases
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Write proofs that leave no hidden cases. Prove a statement for every whole number Prove that n(n + 1) is even for every non-negative whole number n. Checking several values is useful, but your proof must also cover values you have not checked. Exactly one of two consecutive integers is even. In either case the product visibly contains a factor of 2. Work through the example 1. Every whole number is either even or odd. These two cases do not overlap, and there is no third parity case. 2. If n is even, write n = 2k for a non-negative whole number k. Then n(n + 1) = 2k(2k + 1), which is 2 times a whole number. 3. If n is odd, write n = 2k + 1 for a non-negative whole number k. Then n + 1 = 2k + 2 = 2(k + 1), so n(n + 1) = 2(2k + 1)(k + 1), again 2 times a whole number. 4. Thus the product is even in every case. The first case includes n = 0, whose product is 0 and is even. Answer. n(n + 1) is even for every non-negative whole number n. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. Do not copy only the answer. items.title: Start with the structure that limits the choices
items.chapter: Choose a strategy, then learn from the decision
items.transcript: This section is called Start with the structure that limits the choices. Read the request and identify the strongest restriction. A fixed total may suggest contributions or a baseline. A product may suggest prime factors. An ordering condition may suggest positions or cases. A repeated process may suggest an invariant, a reverse route or a state. These are invitations to investigate, not rules that guarantee a particular method. SEE IT Let one restriction create the search space For positive whole-number side lengths and area 24, the four factor pairs are complete, up to exchanging the two sides. Requiring a perimeter of 20 then selects only the 4-by-6 rectangle. Choose a first step that reduces uncertainty. Write the possible endings, recover a hidden total, mark the legal connections or state an equation with named quantities. A092, A102 and A114 reward combining restrictions instead of developing one clue in isolation. After using a clue, keep it visible so that later choices cannot accidentally break it. Before starting a long calculation, estimate the size of the search. Can one variable be bounded? Can symmetry identify equivalent cases? Can a complement reduce the work? If a method begins to create a large uncontrolled list, pause and identify what makes the cases different. Changing representation is often more useful than pushing the same arithmetic harder. Record a short reason for your chosen method so you can assess that decision afterwards. Before moving on, open your notebook. Write the facts already established, the cases already handled and the next decision that remains. This makes it possible to return without restarting or repeating the same failed branch. Under time pressure, a well-marked partial solution is more useful than scattered calculations whose purpose has been forgotten. items.title: Use answer information, then check independently
items.chapter: Choose a strategy, then learn from the decision
items.transcript: This section is called Use answer information, then check independently. Use answer options as additional information when they are available, while still checking the original conditions. An option can be substituted or eliminated, but recognising a familiar-looking number is not evidence. For a numerical-response question, read the exact requested output. You may have found an intermediate digit, probability, count or measurement and still need one final operation to answer the question. Check in a way that attacks a different possible error. Substitute a candidate into every equation. Compare a direct count with a complement. Check an optimum by separating its bound from its witness. Recompute a total from disjoint parts instead of repeating the same sequence of additions. items.title: Choose a strategy, then learn from the decision
items.chapter: Choose a strategy, then learn from the decision
items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Choose a strategy, then learn from the decision. Use the larger number to organise a count Choose two different numbers from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Order does not matter. How many choices have a sum of at least 9? Use a complete classification, then check by a different count. Use only cells with smaller < larger. The four highlighted cells include both pairs summing exactly to 9, so the threshold is handled correctly. Work through the example 1. Call the smaller number a and the larger number b, so a < b. This convention prevents counting a reversed pair twice. 2. If b ≤ 4, even the two largest possible numbers are 3 and 4, whose sum is 7. No such pair qualifies. 3. If b = 5, then a + 5 ≥ 9 forces a = 4, giving (4, 5). If b = 6, then a ≥ 3 gives (3, 6), (4, 6) and (5, 6). The count is 1 + 3 = 4. 4. For an independent complement check, there are 6  times  5  divided by  2 = 15 unordered pairs altogether. Of the pairs with sum at most 8, 5 have smaller number 1, 4 have smaller number 2, and 2 have smaller number 3; there are no others. That is 11 pairs. 5. The complement gives 15 - 11 = 4, agreeing with the direct classification. Both methods include sum 9, because “at least 9” includes the boundary. Answer. 4 choices: {3, 6}, {4, 5}, {4, 6} and {5, 6}. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. Do not copy only the answer.
